_about: multi-model-team config. Backends (CLIs) and agents are first-class and individually enable/disable-able; routes pick a backend per task (first match wins). Edit this file to add a CLI, flip a backend/agent on or off, or change an agent's role. After editing agents, run node src/lib/gen-agents.mjs to regenerate agents/*.md.

defaults._comment: preset biases tier (budget|balanced|premium). fallback is the final hop. quota_fallback is the ordered backend chain tried when the chosen backend is unavailable/exhausted — a DISABLED backend in this chain is simply skipped, so you can turn one off without editing the chain.
defaults._native_models_note: The SINGLE place a routing tier becomes a concrete Claude model — used by the router, /team and /reasoning so native model choice is configured in one spot instead of three. `high` is the tier a route uses to ask for the strongest model without naming it.

team._comment: PIPELINE knobs for /team — nothing here chooses a backend any more. WHO does each job is decided ENTIRELY by the role staffing (see `roles` below): the user's role spec, with every unstaffed job falling back to Claude. 'verify'/'max_fix_loops' tune the verify->fix loop; 'relay_model' is the model the thin CLI-relay agents run on; 'mode':"writable" makes every run writable without the --writable flag. Precedence: built-in default < this section < per-invocation args.

roles._comment: The /team STAFFING system — the ONE place that decides which backend does which job (there is no separate auto-assignment panel any more). Vocabulary mirrors oh-my-claudecode's staged pipeline. A role says WHAT a worker is for; the backend says WHICH model runs it. They are independent: any role can run on any backend (`impl:opencode:2` and `impl:claude:1` are both fine), which is the whole point — you pick the model per job, not per stage.
roles._spec_note: Role spec syntax for /team: `role:backend:count` groups, comma-separated inside a role, semicolon-separated between roles. Example: `orch:claude:2;impl:opencode:1,claude:2;review:codex:2`. `backend:count` and `count:backend` are both accepted. A backend-only spec (`5:gemini,2:claude`) still works and means 'staff these as the EXECUTORS' — the fix stage follows them and every other job falls back to Claude.
roles._fallback_note: ANY job the user did not staff runs on `default_backend` (Claude) at that role's catalog `tier`, which is what picks the Claude model via defaults.native_models. Nothing is auto-assigned to a CLI backend — a CLI runs only where you put it.
roles._stages_note: Stages run in this order; every role belongs to exactly one. `plan`/`prd`/`exec` are decomposed into subtasks; `verify` and `fix` are the pipeline's own review/repair machinery (they act on exec results, they are not planned work). A plan/prd stage nobody staffed is skipped. This is OMC's `team-plan -> team-prd -> team-exec -> team-verify -> team-fix`.
roles._defaults_note: Used when a role is named with no backend, or a backend with no count.
roles._core_note: The three jobs the pipeline ALWAYS needs. Each unstaffed one runs on `default_backend` with `count` workers at its catalog tier. `follows` borrows another role's staffing instead of defaulting — the fixer follows the executor, so `impl:opencode:2` puts fixes on opencode too, and a fix always goes back to the backend that did the work.
roles._catalog_note: One entry per OMC agent, plus `fixer` for the fix stage (OMC staffs team-fix with executor/debugger; naming it lets you assign that stage directly). `tier` is the DEFAULT tier for the role and matches OMC's model choice for that agent (opus->high, sonnet->standard, haiku->cheap); it resolves per-backend through the normal model ladder, so `high` on agy means agy's strongest model, not Opus. Aliases are what a user may type; the canonical name is the key.

explore.desc: Scan the codebase and report what exists, where, and how it fits together.

planner.desc: Decompose the task into an ordered, runnable task graph.

architect.desc: Decide system boundaries, interfaces and structural trade-offs.

analyst.desc: Turn a vague ask into explicit requirements and acceptance criteria.

critic.desc: Challenge the scope and plan; surface what was assumed or missed.

designer.desc: Build or restyle UI — components, layout, visual polish.

debugger.desc: Isolate a failure to its root cause and fix it.

tracer.desc: Trace causality through a system with competing hypotheses and evidence.

test-engineer.desc: Write and harden tests — unit, integration, e2e, regression.

code-simplifier.desc: Simplify and tighten code without changing behaviour.

writer.desc: Write user-facing docs, READMEs and comments.

document-specialist.desc: Pull in and digest external documentation and references.

scientist.desc: Run data analysis and empirical investigation.

git-master.desc: Handle git surgery — atomic commits, rebases, history repair.

verifier.desc: Check each result against its acceptance criterion with evidence.

code-reviewer.desc: Review the change for correctness, edge cases and quality.

security-reviewer.desc: Audit for vulnerabilities, unsafe patterns and leaked secrets.

qa-tester.desc: Exercise the running software the way a user would.

fixer.desc: Apply bounded fixes for defects verification found.

reasoning._comment: Roles + defaults for the /reasoning Fusion pipeline. 'panel' is YOUR configurable list of reasoning models — editing it changes which models participate in /reasoning by default (e.g. add a 4th model: ['opus','sonnet','gemini','codex']; or go CLI-only: ['gemini','codex']). Each token runs the SAME question in parallel; see docs/REASONING.md for the full token vocabulary (opus/sonnet/haiku/gemini/flash/codex and their aliases). 'judge' compares the panel into structured analysis; 'synthesizer' writes the unified answer (both 'native:<tier>' or a bare tier/backend token). 'cap' bounds total panelists. 'tier_models' maps a tier to a concrete native model; 'relay_model' is the model the thin CLI-relay agents run on. The panel (and judge/synthesizer) are user-configurable here; overridable further per-invocation via a panel spec like '2:gemini,opus,codex', or in-session 'judge with sonnet'. Precedence: built-in default < this section < per-invocation.

backends._comment: Each key is a backend name a route can target. 'enabled' gates use (disabled -> skipped, falls through to the next hop / native). 'kind' selects the invoker in src/lib/backends.mjs ('gemini' (agy) and 'codex' are implemented; 'opencode' is a config stub with no invoker yet, so enabling it simply falls through until an invoker is added). 'writable_extra' = flags used INSTEAD of 'extra' in /team --writable mode (full-auto).

agy._writable_note: Flags used INSTEAD of `extra` in /team --writable mode (full-auto: agy may write files + run commands in its worktree cwd). agy's --dangerously-skip-permissions already lets it act; the writable lane only differs by running in the worktree cwd. Same flags here = no sandbox swap needed for agy, just cwd.
agy._models_note: Tier -> model id. These are the ID-form names from the LEFT column of `agy models` (verified live: `--model gemini-3.7-flash-high` answers). The right column's display strings ("Gemini 3.7 Flash (High)") are also accepted, but the ids are preferred — no spaces or parens to survive a command line. All three tiers are ONE generation (3.7 Flash) at low/medium/high reasoning, so changing tier changes effort, not model family; no tier reaches Gemini Pro any more, which is what the pro/pro-hi aliases are for. Any tier key is allowed; a route asking for a tier this map lacks falls back through default_tier -> standard -> cheap. Run `agy models` to see the current list.
agy._aliases_note: Short handles usable anywhere a model is named (roster tiers, --model, MMT_MODEL_AGY).

The flash handles track whatever generation the TIERS use, so `--model flash` never silently means an older generation than an unpinned call. pro/pro-hi are kept deliberately: the tiers no longer reach Gemini Pro, so these are the only way to ask for it.
agy._timeout_note: hard_timeout (run.mjs SIGKILL) is kept ABOVE agy's own --print-timeout (29m < 30m) so agy self-terminates and emits its partial answer BEFORE run.mjs hard-kills it — the graceful path (exit 0, partial output kept) instead of the SIGKILL path (output discarded, native fallback). Heavy /team --writable component jobs (real implementation, not review) can run 20min+; raised from 15m/14m to 30m/29m. NOTE: the relay's own Bash-tool timeout caps at 600000ms (10min) — for jobs beyond that the relay loses its stdout but RECOVERS via the status file (run.mjs keeps running to hard_timeout; relaySucceeded() reclaims a state:done result). Keep --print-timeout exactly 1m under hard_timeout if you retune either.
agy._cost_note: tunable estimate, USD per 1000 output chars — for the HUD cost figure only

codex._writable_note: Flags used INSTEAD of `extra` in /team --writable mode. Full-auto: `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` lets codex write files, run commands, and use the network — confined to the worktree cwd the orchestrator passes via --cwd. Drop --skip-git-repo-check since a worktree IS a git repo.
codex._models_note: Tier -> model id, passed as `-m <id>`. Any tier key is allowed; a tier this map lacks resolves through default_tier -> standard -> cheap, so a `high` route lands on `standard` until you add a `high` entry. Leave the map EMPTY to use whatever ~/.codex/config.toml defaults to. `model_aliases` gives short handles usable in --model / MMT_MODEL_CODEX.
codex._auth_note: Credential failures are matched BEFORE quota patterns so an expired login is reported as an auth error (fix: `codex login`) instead of being mislabelled a credit limit — a live probe returned `401 … invalid_api_key` and the broad quota list swallowed it.
codex._timeout_note: 30m to match agy — a full-auto /team --writable codex job (real implementation, not just review) can run 20min+; raised from 15m. codex has no self-timeout flag (no --print-timeout equivalent), so run.mjs's hard_timeout is the ONLY ceiling: at expiry the codex process is SIGKILLed, its partial output discarded, and the subtask falls back to native. The relay's Bash-tool timeout caps at 600000ms (10min); for longer jobs the relay recovers the result via the status file (relaySucceeded reclaims a state:done run.mjs writes after the relay's tool already returned).
codex._cost_note: tunable estimate, USD per 1000 output chars — for the HUD cost figure only
codex._note: Invoked as `codex exec <flags> -` with the PROMPT delivered on STDIN (the `-` sentinel), not as a positional arg — sidesteps the Windows .cmd newline-truncation bug (see backends.mjs invokeCodex / PROBES.md). Non-interactive, prints only the final message to stdout (no winpty). models empty = codex's own config.toml default; set per-tier model IDs here to map cheap/standard. `-s read-only` (in `extra`) keeps it from modifying files; `/team --writable` swaps to `writable_extra` (full-auto).

opencode._models_note: INTENTIONALLY EMPTY — opencode runs on whichever model the user configured in opencode itself (`opencode models` lists them, the TUI/config picks the default). An empty map makes the invoker omit --model entirely. Add tier keys here ONLY if you want to pin one, e.g. {"cheap":"opencode/deepseek-v4-flash-free","standard":"opencode/big-pickle"}.
opencode._agent_note: opencode expresses read-only vs full-auto through its AGENT, not a sandbox flag: `plan` is the built-in read-only agent, `build` is the read/write one. `agent` is used in the default lane, `writable_agent` (plus --auto to auto-approve) in /team --writable.
opencode._cwd_flag_note: opencode IGNORES the spawned process's cwd and resolves its own project root — verified live: a --writable dispatch into a worktree wrote the file into the PARENT repo instead. `--dir` is the supported way to point it at a directory and confines writes there, so it is passed whenever /team supplies a --cwd.
opencode._print_logs_note: --print-logs sends opencode's diagnostics to STDERR and leaves STDOUT clean (verified: 8KB stderr, 0 bytes of stdout pollution), so it cannot corrupt the answer. Without it a FAILED run reported only opencode's own banner ('> plan · <model>') as its error, which says nothing: a run whose configured provider was unreachable burned 8 minutes and surfaced that banner. run.mjs reads stderr only on failure, so this is free on the success path and makes the real cause ('Cannot connect to API: Unable to connect') land in failures.log.
opencode._timeout_note: Matches agy/codex so a long /team --writable job isn't SIGKILLed mid-run. opencode has no self-timeout flag, so hard_timeout is the only ceiling.
opencode._cost_note: tunable estimate, USD per 1000 output chars — for the HUD cost figure only. Left at agy's rate since opencode's default model is user-chosen and often free/local.
opencode._note: Invoked as `opencode run <flags>` with the PROMPT on STDIN (opencode reads stdin when no positional message is given) — same reason as codex: a multi-line prompt as an argv element is truncated at the first newline by a Windows .cmd wrapper. Needs NO pty (unlike agy): piped stdout works. The answer is on stdout; the `> plan · <model>` banner and ANSI colour go to stderr.

grok._oneshot_note: `grok -p <PROMPT>` (alias --single) is the headless lane: 'Single-turn prompt. Prints the response to stdout and exits.' Verified live through a plain pipe — needs NO pty, unlike agy. NOTE: `--prompt-file` returned NOTHING through a pipe in testing (it appears to want the TUI), which is why the prompt goes as an argv element instead.
grok._models_note: INTENTIONALLY EMPTY, like opencode: grok runs on whichever model you configured in grok itself (`grok models` lists them and marks the default; ~/.grok/config.toml sets it). An empty map makes the invoker omit -m. To pin per tier, add e.g. {"standard":"grok-4.5"} — `grok-4.5` is xAI's model; a custom endpoint you add to grok's config is also nameable here.
grok._permission_note: Read-only vs full-auto is a PERMISSION MODE here, not a sandbox flag (codex) or an agent name (opencode). Modes: default | acceptEdits | auto | dontAsk | bypassPermissions | plan. VERIFIED LIVE, and the result was surprising: `plan` did NOT block a write — grok created the file anyway — so it is NOT the read-only lane despite the name. `default` is the lane that actually blocks writes: with no TTY to approve a tool call, the call is refused. A pure read/answer task returns normally. BUT THE REFUSAL IS NOT ALWAYS CLEAN — observed live: grok emitted 296 chars of narration, hit a tool call it needed to RUN, and exited 0 with that partial text. run.mjs scores exit-0-plus-output as SUCCESS, so a truncated stub comes back as if it were the answer (an empty-output refusal does fall through loudly; a partial one does not). So: this lane never writes, but it can return an unfinished answer. Treat a read-only grok result as unverified — that is what the /team verify stage is for — and staff grok --writable (bypassPermissions, confined to the worktree) for work that genuinely needs to execute commands. Deny rules were tried too and are NOT sufficient: `--deny Write` blocked the write tool and grok simply routed around it via the terminal.
grok._cwd_flag_note: grok takes an explicit --cwd. Passed alongside the spawn cwd whenever /team supplies one, so a --writable subtask is confined to its worktree (the same belt-and-braces opencode needed).
grok._timeout_note: Matches the other CLIs so a long /team --writable job isn't SIGKILLed mid-run. grok has no self-timeout flag, so hard_timeout is the only ceiling — and since the runChild fix that ceiling now holds even when the kill doesn't land.
grok._cost_note: tunable estimate, USD per 1000 output chars — for the HUD cost figure only.
grok._note: Grok Build (xAI's harness). The binary resolves to a real grok.exe, so Node passes argv straight through with no cmd.exe in between: a multi-line prompt survives as an argv element and is never shell-parsed. KNOWN LIMIT: argv means the Windows ~32k command-line cap applies to very large /team payloads. Like opencode, grok claims no auto-route lane — it runs only where you explicitly staff it, or via the fallback chain.

agents._comment: Claude Code subagents the model can spawn. 'enabled' controls whether agents/<name>.md is generated (disabled -> the .md is removed so Claude Code won't surface it). 'backend'+'tier' set where the agent relays; 'dispatch' is 'route' (let the router decide) or 'forced' (pin backend+tier). 'role' becomes the agent's description (what the model matches on). Regenerate with node src/lib/gen-agents.mjs after editing.

agy.role: Dispatcher for the agy (Gemini) CLI backend — a configurable, equal tool, not a fixed task bucket. WHERE work routes is decided by config/roster.json (routes + tags.txt) and per-subtask /team assignments, not hardcoded here. By the shipped routing config, agy is the default lane for fast, commodity, easily-verifiable work and Gemini's edges: new UI/React components, CSS, SVG/animation, scaffolding, CRUD, REST endpoints, scripts, CLI tools, glue code, SQL, regex, configs, Dockerfiles, unit tests, fixtures, data transforms, web-search/doc summarization, bulk text, and audio/video (Gemini-exclusive). The shipped rules keep reverse-engineering, IL2CPP/protobuf-RE, disasm, FFI/unsafe, injection/hooking, concurrency, protocol/KCP design and other systems-hard work on native Opus — but that is roster policy you can retune, not a property of this agent. Spawning this agent is an explicit choice to run on agy: it relays the task to the CLI and returns the result verbatim; it does not re-route or refuse based on content.

codex.role: Dispatcher for the codex (OpenAI Codex CLI) backend — a configurable, equal tool, not a fixed task bucket. WHERE work routes is decided by config/roster.json (routes + tags.txt) and per-subtask /team assignments, not hardcoded here. By the shipped routing config, codex is the default lane for code review, test-writing, and verification — review a diff/file for correctness, bugs, edge cases and regressions; write or extend unit/integration/e2e test suites; verify an implementation meets its spec — and it serves as the default /team verifier. It runs full-auto in its own git worktree under /team --writable, so it can also make real code changes there. The shipped rules keep reverse-engineering, IL2CPP/protobuf-RE, injection and other systems-hard work on native Opus, but that is roster policy you can retune, not a property of this agent. Spawning this agent is an explicit choice to run on codex: it relays the task to the CLI and returns the result verbatim; it does not re-route or refuse based on content.

opencode.role: Dispatcher for the opencode (OpenCode CLI) backend — a configurable, equal tool, not a fixed task bucket. WHERE work routes is decided by config/roster.json (routes + tags.txt) and per-subtask /team assignments, not hardcoded here. opencode runs on WHICHEVER MODEL THE USER CONFIGURED IN OPENCODE ITSELF (the plugin deliberately passes no model flag), so it is the lane for work you want on your own opencode setup — a local or self-hosted model, a provider Claude/agy/codex don't cover, or simply a third independent opinion for /reasoning panels. By default it claims no auto-route lane, so it runs only when you explicitly pick it: spawning this agent, assigning it in /team, listing it in a /reasoning panel, or when it is reached through the quota-fallback chain. It uses opencode's read-only `plan` agent by default and its read/write `build` agent under /team --writable. Spawning this agent is an explicit choice to run on opencode: it relays the task to the CLI and returns the result verbatim; it does not re-route or refuse based on content.

grok.role: Dispatcher for the grok (Grok Build, xAI's harness) CLI backend — a configurable, equal tool, not a fixed task bucket. WHERE work routes is decided by config/roster.json (routes + tags.txt) and per-subtask /team assignments, not hardcoded here. grok runs on WHICHEVER MODEL IS CONFIGURED IN GROK ITSELF (the plugin passes no model flag by default; `grok models` lists them, and xAI's `grok-4.5` is available alongside any custom endpoint you have configured), so it is the lane for work you want on Grok or on your own grok-configured provider — or simply a further independent opinion for /reasoning panels. By default it claims no auto-route lane, so it runs only when you explicitly pick it: spawning this agent, staffing it in /team (`impl:grok:2`), listing it in a /reasoning panel, or when it is reached through the quota-fallback chain. IMPORTANT: grok's read-only lane blocks writes but is NOT fail-safe — a refused tool call can end the run early, returning a TRUNCATED answer that looks like a complete one (see the roster note). Treat a read-only grok result as unverified, and prefer grok for work that only needs to read and reason. Spawning this agent is an explicit choice to run on grok: it relays the task to the CLI and returns the result verbatim; it does not re-route or refuse based on content.

routes._comment: HARD LINE: RE / injection / binary / systems-hard. ALWAYS Opus, checked first so nothing below can offload these.
routes.name: re-injection-heavy

routes._comment: Deep systems / concurrency / architecture — judgment-critical, not commodity.
routes.name: systems-complex

routes._comment: Gemini-exclusive: A/V must go to agy even if it also carries a judgment word, so it is checked before judgment-coding.
routes.name: multimodal

routes._comment: Judgment coding — ordered ABOVE the commodity agy rules so refactor/bugfix/integration go to Sonnet even when they also mention a button/script/config. (review/unit-test moved to the codex lane just below.)
routes.name: judgment-coding

routes._comment: Codex's lane — code review, test-writing, and verification: code-specialized, checkable work that sits BETWEEN agy-Standard and native-Sonnet. Ordered below judgment-coding (a refactor/bugfix word still wins -> Sonnet) and below the OPUS hard-line/systems rules (those win -> Opus), but ABOVE the commodity agy rules, so a PURE review/test/verify task lands on codex.
routes.name: code-review-test

routes._comment: bulk-ingest BEFORE grounded-research: both match summarize/extract/ingest/scan; the cheap large-input path must win first or a 30k dump would route standard.
routes.name: bulk-ingest

routes._comment: Standard, verifiable coding — most everyday code work.
routes.name: standard-coding

routes._comment: Default when UNCLASSIFIED — prefer sonnet (safe middle), never agy on a guess.
routes.name: catch-all-safe
